title: Turkey, dark meat, roasted, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Dark turkey meat is the portion of the bird that contains more myoglobin than white meat, giving it a richer flavor and darker color. When roasted with the skin on, it stays juicy and flavorful, while the crisp skin adds a pleasant texture. Turkey is a popular source of lean protein, widely used in both festive and everyday dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat comes mainly from the thigh and drumstick, where the muscles work harder than in the breast.
Turkey skin contains beneficial fats that help absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.
Roasting with the skin helps retain moisture, making the meat more tender.
Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
In the United States, turkey is traditionally associated with Thanksgiving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Dark turkey meat provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Higher myoglobin levels mean better iron content, important for blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is high in B12, niacin (B3) and B6, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can benefit heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, turkey has less saturated fat, making it a better choice for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked dark meat may harbor pathogens like Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to turkey proteins.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: If the turkey is brined or smoked, it can contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie density of the skin
items.content: The skin adds extra calories and fat, so those watching weight should moderate its intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted turkey with skin can be served whole, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, or incorporated into hot dishes like pasta and risotto. The skin can be eaten crispy or removed for a leaner option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in a zip‑top bag with the air removed – they keep well for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.
